During a game against the [[2018 Houston Texans season|Houston Texans]] on November 18, 2018, Smith suffered a [[spiral fracture|spiral]] and [[compound fracture|compound]] fracture to his [[tibia]] and [[fibula]] in his right leg when he was sacked by [[Kareem Jackson]] and [[J. J. Watt]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Sessler |first=Marc |date=November 18, 2018 |title=Alex Smith suffers broken leg in Redskins' loss |url=https://www.nfl.com/news/alex-smith-suffers-broken-leg-in-redskins-loss-0ap3000000989183 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181119010956/http://www.nfl.com/news/story/0ap3000000989183/article/redskins-qb-alex-smith-suffers-broken-tibia-fibula |archive-date=November 19, 2018 |access-date=November 18, 2018 |website=NFL.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Williams |first=Charean |date=November 19, 2018 |title=Alex Smith's compound fracture will require 6–8 month recovery |url=https://profootballtalk.nbcsports.com/2018/11/19/alex-smiths-compound-fracture-will-require-6-8-month-recovery/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181120095431/https://profootballtalk.nbcsports.com/2018/11/19/alex-smiths-compound-fracture-will-require-6-8-month-recovery/ |archive-date=November 20, 2018 |access-date=November 20, 2018 |website=Pro Football Talk}}</ref> The injury drew parallels to former Washington quarterback [[Joe Theismann]], who suffered a career-ending leg fracture in a game 33 years to the day prior in 1985.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Stubbs |first=Roma |date=November 18, 2018 |title=Exactly 33 years since his own gruesome injury, Joe Theismann 'just so upset' for Alex Smith |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/sports/redskins/exactly-33-years-since-his-own-gruesome-injury-joe-theismann-just-so-upset-for-alex-smith/2018/11/18/4cace552-eb80-11e8-baac-2a674e91502b_story.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181119185025/https://www.washingtonpost.com/sports/redskins/exactly-33-years-since-his-own-gruesome-injury-joe-theismann-just-so-upset-for-alex-smith/2018/11/18/4cace552-eb80-11e8-baac-2a674e91502b_story.html |archive-date=November 19, 2018 |access-date=November 19, 2018 |newspaper=Washington Post}}</ref> Theismann was also present during the game and witnessed the injury. The game ended with the same score of 23–21 as the one in which Theismann was injured, though the Redskins won the game against the Giants in 1985.

[[File:Alex Smith (45945178521).jpg|thumb|left|Smith following his leg fracture]]
Following the initial surgery, Smith developed life-threatening [[necrotizing fasciitis]] that resulted in [[sepsis]] which required him to undergo 17 surgeries, including eight [[debridement]]s, across four separate hospital stays over a period of nine months.<ref name="ESPNInjury">{{Cite web |last1=Smith |first1=Elizabeth |last2=Bell |first2=Stephania |date=May 1, 2020 |title=Alex Smith's comeback: Inside the fight to save the QB's leg and life |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/29112995/alex-smith-comeback-fight-save-qb-leg-life |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200527151706/https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/29112995/alex-smith-comeback-fight-save-qb-leg-life |archive-date=May 27, 2020 |access-date=May 24, 2020 |website=ESPN.com}}</ref> Doctors had suggested that an amputation above the knee might have been Smith's only option before performing [[skin graft]]s and an operation transferring muscle from his left [[quadriceps]] to save it.<ref name="ESPNInjury" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Gleeson |first=Scott |date=February 1, 2020 |title=Redskins QB Alex Smith says he's 'lucky to be alive' after leg injury, infection |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/sports/nfl/2020/02/01/alex-smith-leg-injury-infection-sepsis-washington-redskins/4632724002/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200213003608/https://www.usatoday.com/story/sports/nfl/2020/02/01/alex-smith-leg-injury-infection-sepsis-washington-redskins/4632724002/ |archive-date=February 13, 2020 |access-date=February 13, 2020 |website=USA TODAY |language=en-US}}</ref>

As a part of his recovery process, Smith wore an [[external fixation]] device for nearly a year.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Gordon |first=Grant |date=December 16, 2018 |title=Redskins' Alex Smith out of hospital, back at home |url=https://www.nfl.com/news/redskins-alex-smith-out-of-hospital-back-at-home-0ap3000001000100 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181216200837/http://www.nfl.com/news/story/0ap3000001000100/article/redskins-alex-smith-out-of-hospital-back-at-home |archive-date=December 16, 2018 |access-date=December 16, 2018 |website=NFL.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Copeland |first=Kareem |date=July 15, 2019 |title=Redskins' Alex Smith has external fixator removed, nearly eight months after leg injury |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/sports/2019/07/15/redskins-alex-smith-has-external-fixator-removed-nearly-eight-months-after-leg-injury/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200818115927/https://www.washingtonpost.com/sports/2019/07/15/redskins-alex-smith-has-external-fixator-removed-nearly-eight-months-after-leg-injury/ |archive-date=August 18, 2020 |access-date=October 17, 2020 |newspaper=Washington Post}}</ref>

====2019 season====
Smith was placed on the team's [[physically unable to perform]] (PUP) reserve list in 2019, missing the entire season.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Fowler |first=Ryan |date=July 24, 2019 |title=Three Redskins Placed On PUP List To Start Training Camp |url=https://www.redskins.com/news/three-redskins-placed-on-pup-list-to-start-training-camp |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200714070717/https://www.redskins.com/news/three-redskins-placed-on-pup-list-to-start-training-camp |archive-date=July 14, 2020 |access-date=October 17, 2020 |website=Redskins.com}}</ref> Despite the severity of the injury which many thought he would never come back from, Smith affirmed his intent to return in early 2020.<ref>{{Cite web |date=February 12, 2020 |title=The Alex Smith comeback attempt: "the first to do it" |url=https://www.hogshaven.com/2020/2/12/21134388/the-alex-smith-comeback-attempt-the-first-to-do-it |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200213003609/https://www.hogshaven.com/2020/2/12/21134388/the-alex-smith-comeback-attempt-the-first-to-do-it |archive-date=February 13, 2020 |access-date=February 13, 2020 |website=Hogs Haven |language=en}}</ref> An ''[[ESPN]]'' documentary following Smith's recovery, ''Project 11'', aired in May 2020.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hall |first=Andy |date=April 28, 2020 |title=E60 Documents NFL QB Alex Smith's Courageous Recovery From Gruesome Leg Injury |url=https://espnpressroom.com/us/press-releases/2020/04/e60-documents-nfl-qb-alex-smiths-courageous-recovery-from-gruesome-leg-injury/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200524075429/https://espnpressroom.com/us/press-releases/2020/04/e60-documents-nfl-qb-alex-smiths-courageous-recovery-from-gruesome-leg-injury/ |archive-date=May 24, 2020 |access-date=May 24, 2020 |website=ESPNPressRoom.com}}</ref>

=== Retirement ===
Despite garnering interest from several teams to claim Smith off waivers,<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Pickman |first=Ben |date=April 22, 2021 |title=Source: Jags Tried to Sign Smith Prior to Retirement |url=https://www.si.com/nfl/2021/04/22/alex-smith-jaguars-contract-offer-offseason |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210507012849/https://www.si.com/nfl/2021/04/22/alex-smith-jaguars-contract-offer-offseason |archive-date=May 7, 2021 |access-date=September 22, 2021 |magazine=Sports Illustrated |language=en-us}}</ref> he announced his retirement on April 19, 2021.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Shook |first=Nick |date=April 19, 2021 |title=Alex Smith announces retirement after 16-year career |url=https://www.nfl.com/news/alex-smith-retires-16-year-career-49ers-chiefs-washington |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210419155905/https://www.nfl.com/news/alex-smith-retires-16-year-career-49ers-chiefs-washington |archive-date=April 19, 2021 |access-date=April 19, 2021 |website=NFL.com}}</ref> In June, Smith was named the winner of the [[George Halas Award]] by the PFWA.<ref>{{Cite web |date=June 7, 2021 |title=Retired QB Alex Smith wins PFWA's George Halas Award for overcoming adversity |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/31585640/retired-qb-alex-smith-wins-pfwa-george-halas-award-overcoming-adversity |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220530002954/https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/31585640/retired-qb-alex-smith-wins-pfwa-george-halas-award-overcoming-adversity |archive-date=May 30, 2022 |access-date=May 30, 2022 |website=ESPN.com |agency=Associated Press}}</ref>

In June 2021, Smith signed a brand partnership with recovery shoe brand [[Oofos]].<ref name="auto5">{{Cite web |last=Verry |first=Peter |date=June 3, 2021 |title=Retired NFL Quarterback Alex Smith Enters Partnership With Recovery Footwear Brand Oofos |url=https://www.yahoo.com/lifestyle/retired-nfl-quarterback-alex-smith-131758965.html |access-date=June 14, 2026 |website=Yahoo! ==Personal life==
Smith married former [[Oakland Raiders]] cheerleader Elizabeth Barry in 2009.<ref name="marriage">{{Cite web |last=Adams |first=Jonathan |date=January 9, 2016 |title=Elizabeth Smith, Alex's Wife: 5 Fast Facts You Need to Know |url=https://heavy.com/sports/2016/01/alex-smith-wife-girlfriend-elizabeth-barry-elizabeth-smith-children-kids-photos-raiders-cheerleader-instagram-twitter-bio-married-who-chiefs-quarterback/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200811195744/https://heavy.com/sports/2016/01/alex-smith-wife-girlfriend-elizabeth-barry-elizabeth-smith-children-kids-photos-raiders-cheerleader-instagram-twitter-bio-married-who-chiefs-quarterback/ |archive-date=August 11, 2020 |access-date=September 20, 2018 |website=Heavy.com}}</ref> They have two sons and a daughter.<ref name="marriage" />

'''Allan Stephen Kennedy''' (born January 8, 1958) is a Canadian former professional [[American football]] player. He played [[offensive tackle]] for the [[San Francisco 49ers]].

He grew up in [[Woodland Hills, California]], where he attended [[El Camino Real High School]]. He then attended [[Washington State University]] to play football. In the [[1981 NFL draft]] he was the 267th pick overall by the [[Washington Redskins]]. He was cut by the Redskins, but was signed by the 49ers. That year, he played three games. However, he didn't play in 1982. The next year, he played in every game, and in 1984, he only missed one game.

Boone''' (born January 11, 1976) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[defensive end]] for 10 seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). Sack Makes a Name for Himself |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2000-apr-18-sp-20825-story.html |access-date=2025-10-22 |website=Los Angeles Times |language=en-US}}</ref> He was selected by the [[Detroit Lions]] in the seventh round of the [[2000 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=2000 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2000/draft.htm |access-date=2023-03-19 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He played [[college football]] at [[Mt. San Antonio College]].

Boone has also played for the [[Chicago Bears]] and [[Kansas City Chiefs]].

==Early life==
Boone attended [[Arthur Hill High School]] in Saginaw, Michigan and was a [[Letterman (sports)|letterman]] in football, basketball, and track and field graduating in 1995. Boone saw time as a fullback his sophomore season which went to the state championship game. He did not play his junior year.<ref>{{Cite news |date=1994-09-01 |title=Saginaw Arthur Hill Top 25 Prep |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/detroit-free-press-saginaw-arthur-hill-t/183435949/ |access-date=2025-10-21 |work=Detroit Free Press |pages=59}}</ref> As a senior, he was nominated all-area honorable mention.<ref>{{Cite news |date=1994-11-26 |title=All-Area Gridders |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-saginaw-news-all-area-gridders/183436417/ |access-date=2025-10-21 |work=The Saginaw News |pages=30}}</ref> Boone qualified for the state meet in the shot put.<ref>{{Cite news |date=1994-05-22 |title=Athletes qualify for state meet. |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-saginaw-news-athletes-qualify-for-st/183436486/ |access-date=2025-10-21 |work=The Saginaw News |pages=44}}</ref> 

Upon graduation, Boone enrolled at [[Central State University]] and was part of the team which won the 1995 NAIA Division I championship in 1995. The school folded the football team after his freshman year. After three years out of football, Boone enrolled at [[Mt. San Antonio College]] where he would earn all-American honors and Defensive Player of the Year All for the [[Mission Conference]].<ref>{{Cite news |date=1999-12-01 |title=JC All Americans 1999 |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/north-county-times-jc-all-americans-1999/183435286/ |access-date=2025-10-22 |work=North County Times |pages=25}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=FAME |first=SAGINAW COUNTY SPORTS HALL OF |date=2024-01-24 |title=Alfonso Boone |url=https://saginawcountysports.org/alfonso-boone/ |access-date=2025-10-22 |website=SAGINAW COUNTY SPORTS HALL OF FAME |language=en-US}}</ref>

'''Alfonso Lanard Marshall''' (born January 17, 1981) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] [[cornerback]] who played for the [[Chicago Bears]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He was selected with the 14th pick of the seventh round in the [[2004 NFL draft]], out of the [[University of Miami]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2004/draft.htm |title=2004 NFL Draft Listing |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en |access-date=2023-05-06}}</ref> 

==Professional career==
Marshall was selected by the [[Chicago Bears]] in the seventh round, with the 215th overall pick, of the [[2004 NFL draft]].<ref name="Pfr">{{cite web | url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/M/MarsAl20.htm | title=Alfonso Marshall | publisher=Pro-Football-Reference | accessdate=24 August 2024}}</ref> He was waived on September 5, and signed to the team's practice squad on  September 7.<ref>{{cite web |last=Mayer |first=Larry |url=http://www.chicagobears.com/news/article-1/Robinson-Forsey-among-Bears-final-cuts/57E0F739-80D5-4950-B8AC-15C1FD3BBAA7 |title=Robinson, Forsey among Bears' final cuts |publisher=Chicagobears.com |accessdate=August 27, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160701104933/http://www.chicagobears.com/news/article-1/Robinson-Forsey-among-Bears-final-cuts/57E0F739-80D5-4950-B8AC-15C1FD3BBAA7 |archive-date=July 1, 2016 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name="Pfr"/> He was promoted to the active roster on September 21. Marshall played in seven games during the 2004 season, recording four solo tackles and three assisted tackles before being placed on injured reserve on November 15, 2004.<ref name="Pfr"/>

He was placed on the [[physically unable to perform]] list on August 30, 2005, and did not appear in any games during the 2005 season. Marshall was waived by the Bears on August 7, 2006.<ref name="Pfr"/>

'''Alfred Hamilton Williams''' (born November 6, 1968) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] and [[defensive end]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[Cincinnati Bengals]], [[San Francisco 49ers]] and [[Denver Broncos]].

==College career==
Williams played linebacker at the [[University of Colorado at Boulder]]. He was a [[unanimous All-American]] pick in 1990, a consensus All-American in 1989 and the 1990 [[Butkus Award]] winner.<ref name="selected">{{cite web|url=http://buffzone.com/news/2008/mar/12/cu-sports-williams-included-on-college-hof/|title=Williams included on college HOF He was elected to the College Football Hall of Fame in 2010. ballot|publisher=DailyCamera.com|date=2008-03-12|access-date=2008-03-12|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://archive.today/20110809203550/http://buffzone.com/news/2008/mar/12/cu-sports-williams-included-on-college-hof/|archive-date=2011-08-09}}</ref> Williams was also the Captain of the 1990 Colorado National Championship Team. He ended his career with the [[Colorado Buffaloes]] with 263 tackles and 35 sacks.<ref name="selected" /> In 2008, he was included on the [[College Football Hall of Fame]] ballot.<ref name="selected" />
Then in 2010, he was elected to the College Football Hall of Fame.

==Professional career==
Williams was selected by the Bengals in the first round (18th pick overall) of the [[1991 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1991 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1991/draft.htm |access-date=2023-05-07 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He was a part of the [[Super Bowl]] champion Denver Broncos in [[Super Bowl XXXII|1997]] and [[Super Bowl XXXIII|1998]]. He was selected as an [[All-Pro]] defensive end in 1996.<ref name="selected" /> He retired from the game after the 1999 season.

==In media ==
From 2006 to 2019, Williams served as an on-air personality for Denver sports radio station [[KKFN]]. In February 2019, Williams left the station and signed with [[iHeartMedia]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.westword.com/news/broncos-radio-flips-to-rush-limbaugh-freedom-937-11405071|title=Broncos Radio to Be Replaced by Rush Limbaugh, "Freedom" Talk|last=Roberts|first=Michael|date=2019-07-09|website=Westword|access-date=2019-07-15}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.9news.com/article/sports/nfl/denver-broncos/orange-and-blue-radio-gives-way-to-expanded-broncos-coverage-on-koa/73-b203b148-0745-45a5-b9ab-933abd41ac23|title=Orange and Blue radio gives way to expanded Broncos coverage on KOA|website=KUSA|date=8 July 2019 |access-date=2019-07-15}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.9news.com/article/sports/nfl/denver-broncos/mike-klis/big-al-leaves-the-fan-headed-for-koa/73-5d9dfa70-d160-4712-a640-bc8a0d5d9f9f|title=Big Al leaves The Fan, headed for KOA|website=KUSA|access-date=2019-07-15}}</ref> where he began hosting [[KOA (AM)|KOA]]'s new afternoon drive show ''Big Al & JoJo'' beginning September 3, 2019.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://radioinsight.com/headlines/180093/koa-completes-schedule-revamp-with-long-awaited-addition-of-alfred-williams/|title=KOA Completes Schedule Revamp With Long Awaited Addition Of Alfred Williams|date=2019-08-28|website=RadioInsight|language=en-US|access-date=2019-11-05}}</ref>

'''Aleksandar Stepanovich''' ({{IPAc-en|s|t|ɛ|ˈ|p|ɑː|n|oʊ-|v|ɪ|tʃ}} {{respell|steh|PAHN|o|vitch}}; born September 25, 1981) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Center (American football)|center]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He was selected by the [[Arizona Cardinals]] in the fourth round of the [[2004 NFL draft]].<ref name=cardinals /> He played [[college football]] for the [[Ohio State Buckeyes football|Ohio State Buckeyes]]. Stepanovich has also played for the [[Cincinnati Bengals]], [[Atlanta Falcons]], and [[Pittsburgh Steelers]].

==Early life==
In 2000, Stepanovich graduated from [[Berea High School]] in [[Berea, Ohio]]. A gifted athlete who's drive made him one of the best offensive lineman in the country during his junior and senior years, Stepanovich made numerous All-American teams along with being well decorated with numerous awards as a high school football player. He was also an accomplished [[Scholastic wrestling|wrestler]] in high school, winning the heavyweight state championship in 2000 and runner-up in 1999. He was a nationally ranked wrestler throughout high school, with multiple MVP's in national and state tournaments, along with two Pioneer Conference MVP's. He was also known for his generosity to helping the youth in his area. Stepanovich's legacy will be forever etched in Ohio with multiple Life Achievement awards for sports and giving back to his community. In Oct. 2023 the Ohio Chapter of the National Wrestling Hall of Fame inducted Stepanovich into the National Wrestling Hall of Fame in Stillwater, Oklahoma as its unanimous selection as its "Outstanding American".

==College career==
Well respected amongst his teammates, known for his work ethic and toughness, regarded as one of the top centers in [[college football]] during 2001 and [[2002 Ohio State Buckeyes football team|2002 at The Ohio State University]], he shifted to [[Guard (American football)|guard]] in his senior campaign and started 26 games during his college football career and was an All-Big Ten and All-American performer. A four-year lettermen while at OSU, his career culminated with a Buckeye tree being planted in his honor in Buckeye Grove joining all other first-team All-Americans at OSU.

==Professional career==
===Arizona Cardinals===
The Cardinals selected him in the fourth round of the [[2004 NFL draft]] and Stepanovich moved into the [[starting lineup]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2004/draft.htm |title=2004 NFL Draft Listing |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en |access-date=2023-05-06}}</ref><ref name=cardinals>[http://www.azcardinals.com/team/bio.php?PRKey=36 Arizona Cardinals bio] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060420143716/http://www.azcardinals.com/team/bio.php?PRKey=36 |date=April 20, 2006 }}</ref> He started every game for the Cardinals in [[2004 NFL season|2004]] without missing a single offensive snap and made several All-Rookie teams, along with being the first rookie center in franchise history to start all 16 games.<ref name=cardinals /> He continued as a starter for much of 2005 and 2006 before going on [[injured reserve]].

The Cardinals elected not to tender him an offer for 2007, making him an [[unrestricted free agent]].

===Cincinnati Bengals===
In March, the [[Cincinnati Bengals]] signed Stepanovich to a one-year deal for 2007. He played in all 16 games and started 5.

===Atlanta Falcons===
On March 10, 2008, Stepanovich was signed by the [[Atlanta Falcons]] to a three-year deal. He was released on June 17, 2009.

===Pittsburgh Steelers===
Stepanovich signed with the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]] on August 10, 2009. He was [[Waivers (American football)|waived]] on August 31.
Injuries forced his time in Pittsburgh and career short.

'''Alexander Wright''' (born July 19, 1967) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[wide receiver]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[Dallas Cowboys]], [[Los Angeles Raiders]] and [[St. Louis Rams]]. He was a two-time winner of the NFL's "Fastest Man" competition. He played [[college football]] at [[Auburn University]].

==Early life==
Wright attended [[Albany High School (Albany, Georgia)|Albany High School]], where he focused on [[track and field]] until his senior season, when he made the [[American football|football]] team. He played at [[wide receiver]] and [[cornerback]], where his athletic ability allowed him to cover opposing players one-on-one without any additional support.

==College career==
He accepted a football scholarship from [[Auburn University]]. He was initially a [[defensive back]], but because of his poor tackling and lack of run support abilities, he was moved to [[wide receiver]] as a sophomore. As a junior in his first start, he faced the [[University of Tennessee]], tallying 3 receptions for 108 yards, including a 75-yard [[touchdown]]. In the season, he registered 12 receptions for 279 yards and 2 [[touchdown]]s.

Wright developed slowly on the offensive side of the ball and didn't see much playing time, until becoming a starter as a senior after replacing the graduated [[Lawyer Tillman]]. In the season opener against the [[University of the Pacific (United States)|University of the Pacific]], he registered single-game school records with 263 receiving yards (52.6 average) and 4 [[touchdown]]s. Against the [[University of Tennessee]], he collected four receptions for 129 yards and one [[touchdown]].

He had an outstanding game against the [[University of Alabama]], recording 7 receptions for 143 yards in a 30–20 victory over unbeaten Alabama, in the season finale and first [[Iron Bowl]] to be played at [[Jordan–Hare Stadium]].<ref>{{cite web | last=Moran | first=Malcolm | title=COLLEGE FOOTBALL; Alabama Tripped Up By Auburn | website=The New York Times | date=1989-12-03 | url=https://www.nytimes.com/1989/12/03/sports/college-football-alabama-tripped-up-by-auburn.html | access-date=2025-08-05}}</ref> After finishing the season with 30 receptions (led the team) for 714 yards (led the team) and 6 receiving [[touchdown]]s (led the team) in a ground oriented offense, he received the [[Shug Jordan]] Award as the team's outstanding senior football player.

Wright finished in the school's all-time top ten career receiving list with 56 receptions for 1,320 yards and 11 [[touchdown]]s. He still holds the record with a career average of 23.57 yards per reception.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.auburntigers.com/sports/m-footbl/spec-rel/082806aab.html |title=AUBURN VS. WASHINGTON STATE PREVIEW |publisher=University of Auburn |date=August 28, 2006 |access-date=March 30, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180416134952/http://www.auburntigers.com/sports/m-footbl/spec-rel/082806aab.html |archive-date=April 16, 2018 |url-status=dead }}</ref> One-out-of-five of his 56 receptions went for [[touchdown]] with an average distance of over 57 yards. Of his 11 [[touchdown]] receptions, 6 were longer than 50 yards. He also scored in 4 out of the 12 times he ran a [[Reverse (American football)|reverse run]].

He also practiced [[track and field]]. In 1988, he won the [[Southeastern Conference]] title in both the [[55 meters]] and the [[200 meters]], becoming only the second athlete in conference history to be named [[All-American]] in three events ([[55 meters]], [[200 meters]] and [[4 × 100 metres relay]]). His time of 6.18 seconds in the [[55 meters]], at the time tied him with [[Bo Jackson]] as the sixth fastest sprinter in school history.

===Dallas Cowboys===
Wright was selected by the [[Dallas Cowboys]] in the second round (26th overall) of the [[1990 NFL draft]], the first [[wide receiver]] to be chosen and the first pick of the round.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1990 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1990/draft.htm |access-date=2023-05-24 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> Although he was considered a raw football player, he was also seen as a gifted athlete with elite speed.

He was intended to become a deep threat [[wide receiver]], to complement [[running back]] [[Emmitt Smith]], chosen in the first round of the same draft. As well as Smith, he also had a long (40 days) rookie contract holdout, that forced him to miss most of training camp and the first two preseason games.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1696&dat=19900826&id=ZvgaAAAAIBAJ&pg=6808,4369493 |title=Wright, Solomon end their holdouts for the Cowboys |work=Daily News |date=August 26, 1990 |access-date=March 30, 2022}}</ref> In the second game against the [[New York Giants]] he returned a kickoff for a 90-yard [[touchdown]].

In [[1991 NFL season|1991]], he was a starter at [[wide receiver]] in the first 8 games, before being passed on the depth chart by rookie [[Alvin Harper]]. He displayed his talent on [[special teams]] as a [[kickoff returner]], ranking third in the league and second in the [[National Football Conference|NFC]]. Against the [[Phoenix Cardinals]] he had a 71-yard kickoff return. On December 22, [[1991 NFL season|1991]], he set the record for the longest play in Cowboys history, with a 102-yard kick off return against the [[Atlanta Falcons]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/blog/dallas/cowboys/post/_/id/4674611/bryan-mccann-is-player-of-the-week |title=Bryan McCann is Player of the Week |work=ESPN.com |date=November 16, 2010 |access-date=March 30, 2022}}</ref> {{As of|2018}}, he and [[Mel Renfro]] are the only Cowboys with multiple kick return touchdowns.

Wright was one of the fastest players in the league, winning the [[NFL]]'s "Fastest Man" competition in 1992 and 1993. In May [[1991 NFL season|1991]], he was timed to have run the [[40-yard dash]] in 4.14 seconds.<ref>{{cite web|last=Smith |first=Timothy W. |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1991/06/30/sports/football-notebook-browns-won-t-be-built-in-a-season.html |title=Browns Won't Be Built in a Season |publisher=NY Times |date=January 30, 1991 |access-date=March 30, 2022}}</ref> He was also the strongest [[wide receiver]] on the team.

He did not develop as well as expected, however, and when later asked about his performance, he admitted "I was never a polished package". At the end of the [[1991 NFL season|1991 season]], the Cowboys began looking for trade offers. On October 13, [[1992 NFL season|1992]], he was traded to the [[Los Angeles Raiders]] in exchange for a fourth-round draft pick (#96-[[Ron Stone (American football)|Ron Stone]]), when he still had no receptions following the first five games of the season.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1842&dat=19921014&id=3E4eAAAAIBAJ&pg=6066,1996337 |title=Cowboys deal Wright |publisher=Times Daily |date=October 14, 1992 |access-date=March 30, 2022}}</ref>

===Los Angeles Raiders===
Wright was acquired to complement [[Tim Brown (American football)|Tim Brown]] and [[Willie Gault]] in the team's speed-driven offense. In [[1993 NFL season|1993]], he became a full-time starter and had his most productive season, recording 27 receptions for 462 yards. During the final game of that season and with the Raiders trailing the Denver Broncos 23–30, he caught the game-tying touchdown pass from [[Jeff Hostetler]] and the Raiders went on to win the game 33–30, while earning a spot in the playoffs.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.raiders.com/common/article.aspx?id%3D1270 |title=Oakland Raiders - Raiders Drop Broncos into Playoff Pressure Cooker |access-date=March 30, 2022 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081114190425/http://www.raiders.com/common/article.aspx?id=1270 |archive-date=November 14, 2008}}</ref>

In [[1994 NFL season|1994]], he was sidelined for most of training camp with a calf injury he suffered in the first week of activity, but still managed to keep his starting position.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1994-08-19-sp-28997-story.html |title=Wright Might Be on Way Out |newspaper=LA Times |date=August 19, 1994 |access-date=March 30, 2022}}</ref> During his time with the Raiders, [[sportscaster]] [[Chris Berman]] nicknamed him "If Loving You Is Wrong I Don't Want to Be" Wright.

===St. Louis Rams===
On March 22, [[1995 NFL season|1995]], he was signed as a [[free agent]] by the [[St. Louis Rams]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1995/03/23/sports/transactions-192095.html |title=Transactions |publisher=NY Times |date=March 23, 1995 |access-date=March 30, 2022}}</ref> A bulging disk in his lower back forced him to miss the last 8 games of the season.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=2199&dat=19951013&id=WJwyAAAAIBAJ&pg=4661,6592167 |title=Rams' Wright to have surgery |publisher=Lawrence Journal-World |date=October 13, 1995 |access-date=March 30, 2022}}</ref> The next year his back problems resurfaced and he was limited to 3 games.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1893&dat=19960905&id=EzEjAAAAIBAJ&pg=6854,8909419 |title=Rams pickup former KC offensive lineman, ex-Bear defensive back |publisher=The Southeast Missourian |date=September 5, 1996 |access-date=March 30, 2022}}</ref> He retired after the [[1996 NFL season|1996 season]], for health reasons related to his back.

==Coaching career==
In 1999, Wright earned the [[Master of Arts]] in sports management from [[Lindenwood University]]. In 2002, he served as the interim head coach and general manager of the [[RiverCity Rage|River City Renegades]], a [[National Indoor Football League]] team.

In 2003, he served as the wide receiver coach for [[Francis Howell North High School]] in [[St. Charles, Missouri]]. In 2004, he was the wide receiver coach for [[West Texas A&M University]]. In 2005, he was hired to be the [[offensive coordinator]] at [[Greensboro College]] in [[Greensboro, North Carolina]]. He was the offensive coordinator for [[Southwestern Assemblies of God University]] in [[Waxahachie, Texas]]. He then took a role as the [[athletic director]] and head football coach at San Jacinto Christian Academy in [[Amarillo, Texas]], in which he served from 2008 t o 2010. He also assisted with the track team.

Wright later moved to [[San Antonio]] for his ministry. He is the current President and CEO for Alexander Wright Ministries in Amarillo. He is also a pastor at Cornerstone Church in San Antonio.

'''Alfred William Fincher''' (born August 15, 1983) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He was selected by the [[New Orleans Saints]] in the third round of the [[2005 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=2005 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2005/draft.htm |access-date=2023-05-07 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He played [[college football]] for the [[Connecticut Huskies football|Connecticut Huskies]].

Fincher was also a member of the [[Detroit Lions]], [[Washington Redskins]], and [[New York Sentinels]].

==Professional career==

===New Orleans Saints===
In 2006, Fincher played in six games for the New Orleans Saints and recorded nine [[Tackle (football move)|tackles]].

Fincher played in seven games for the [[New Orleans Saints]] in [[2007 New Orleans Saints season|2007]], recording three tackles.  He was placed on [[injured reserve]] on November 4, 2007 due to a [[concussion]], ending his season.  He was waived from injured reserve on November 29. He has inspired his cousin Travis Fincher while playing for the 'SR Colts', during the 2007-08 season.

===Detroit Lions===
On March 27, 2008, Fincher was signed by the [[Detroit Lions]].  However, he was released on July 27 after linebacker [[Teddy Lehman]] was re-signed.

===Washington Redskins===
On July 31, 2008, Fincher was signed by the [[Washington Redskins]]. He re-signed with the Redskins on March 10, 2009. He was waived on August 30.

==Personal life==
Fincher works as a fisherman in the Bahamas.

'''Alfred Donnell Jenkins''' (born January 25, 1952) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[wide receiver]] for the [[Birmingham Americans]] in 1974 and nine seasons for the [[Atlanta Falcons]] from 1975 through 1983. Jenkins was selected to the [[Pro Bowl]] during the 1980 and 1981 seasons and is considered the most successful [[National Football League]] (NFL) player from the short-lived  [[World Football League]] (WFL).<ref name="ajc930727"/>

Jenkins played [[college football]] in Atlanta for the [[Morris Brown Wolverines football|Morris Brown Wolverines]] and was not selected in the [[1974 NFL draft]]. He received a tryout and signed with the WFL's [[Birmingham Americans]]. He scored 14 touchdowns and caught 62 passes for 1,471 yards while helping the Americans win the WFL's only championship that season. After the Americans folded, Jenkins signed with the Falcons on April 9, 1975.<ref>{{cite | last=Harvin | first=Al | title=People in Sports | date=1975-04-10 | issn=0362-4331 | url=https://www.nytimes.com/1975/04/10/archives/people-in-sports-clemson-five-gets-new-coach.html | language=en-US | access-date=2026-03-10 | page=}}</ref> He became a mainstay at wide receiver, starting every game in each of his NFL seasons (with the exception of 1978, in which he played only one game before suffering a broken collarbone).  Jenkins led the NFL in receiving yards (1,358) and receiving touchdowns (13) in the 1981 season.<ref>{{cite web |last=Rosenberg |first=I.J. |date=2016-11-18 |title=Whatever happened to: Alfred Jenkins |url=https://www.ajc.com/sports/football/whatever-happened-alfred-jenkins/rr09H3OGbkkFXLEbEspwVI/ |access-date=2026-03-10 |website=The Atlanta Journal-Constitution}}</ref>

Tight ends coach | highlights = *[[Super Bowl champion]] ([[Super Bowl XXVII|XXVII]]) * 2× [[College football national championships in NCAA Division I FBS|National champion]] ([[1983 Miami Hurricanes football team|1983]], [[1987 Miami Hurricanes football team|1987]]) | statlabel1 = [[Reception (gridiron football)|Reception]]s | statvalue1 = 48 | statlabel2 = Receiving yards | statvalue2 = 450 | statlabel3 = Receiving [[touchdown]]s | statvalue3 = 2 | pfr = RobeAl00 }} '''Alfredo Roberts''' (born March 17, 1965) is an American [[American football|football]] coach and former [[tight end]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL), who serves as the [[tight ends coach]] for the [[New York Jets]]. He played for the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] and [[Dallas Cowboys]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Miami Hurricanes football|Miami Hurricanes]]. ==Early life== Roberts attended [[South Plantation High School]]. As a senior [[tight end]], he received All-city and second-team All-state honors. He helped his team win 2 consecutive city championships. In [[baseball]], he was a second-team All-state [[catcher]]/[[first baseman]] as a senior. He led his team in hitting in two of his three seasons. ==College career== Roberts accepted a football scholarship from the [[University of Miami]]. In 1983, he was [[Redshirt (college sports)|redshirted]], when head coach [[Howard Schnellenberger]] led the team to a National Championship. As a freshman, he was a backup [[tight end]] behind [[Willie Smith (tight end)|Willie Smith]]. The next year, he was a third-string [[tight end]], after being passed on the depth chart by [[Charles Henry (American football)|Charles Henry]].{{Cite web |title=UM's Roberts Relishes Second Chance |url=http://articles.sun-sentinel.com/1986-03-09/sports/8601140775_1_tight-end-alfredo-roberts-charles-henry |access-date=February 5, 2018 |archive-date=July 22, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180722011319/http://articles.sun-sentinel.com/1986-03-09/sports/8601140775_1_tight-end-alfredo-roberts-charles-henry |url-status=dead }} As a junior, he was used as a backup blocking [[tight end]] behind Henry, increasing his receiving production to 10 receptions for 105 yards and 2 [[touchdown]]s. As a senior in 1987, he shared the starting position with Henry,{{Cite web |title=Knee Injury Will Keep Henry Out |url=http://articles.sun-sentinel.com/1987-11-16/sports/8702060268_1_charles-henry-knee-alfredo-roberts |access-date=February 5, 2018 |archive-date=July 21, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180721221924/http://articles.sun-sentinel.com/1987-11-16/sports/8702060268_1_charles-henry-knee-alfredo-roberts |url-status=dead }} making 13 receptions for 137 yards and one [[touchdown]], as part of a 12-0 undefeated team, that won the National Championship under head coach [[Jimmy Johnson (American football coach)|Jimmy Johnson]]. He finished his career with 29 receptions for 296 yards and 4 [[touchdown]]s, while playing on 3 bowl teams (two [[Fiesta Bowl]]s, one [[Sugar Bowl]] and one [[Orange Bowl]]). ==Professional career== ===Kansas City Chiefs=== Roberts was selected by the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] in the eighth-round (197th overall) of the [[1988 NFL draft]].{{Cite web |title=1988 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1988/draft.htm |access-date=September 23, 2023 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}{{Cite web |title=Redskins sign top draft picks |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1298&dat=19880718&id=rv9NAAAAIBAJ&sjid=1osDAAAAIBAJ&pg=6978,3118874&hl=en |access-date=February 5, 2018}} As a rookie, he started the first 7 games, before being limited with a shoulder injury that required arthroscopic surgery in the offseason. He was replaced in the starting lineupe with [[Jonathan Hayes]]. In [[1989 NFL season|1989]], he was a backup behind Hayes, making 8 receptions for 55 yards and one [[touchdown]]. In [[1990 NFL season|1990]], he started 13 games, posting 11 receptions for 119 yards ===Dallas Cowboys=== On March 18, [[1991 NFL season|1991]], he was signed in [[Plan B free agency]] by the [[Dallas Cowboys]], reuniting with his former [[University of Miami]] head coach [[Jimmy Johnson (American football coach)|Jimmy Johnson]]. He was used as a blocking [[tight end]] behind [[Jay Novacek]], helping [[Emmit Smith]] lead the league with 365 carries for 1,563 rushing yards. In [[1992 NFL season|1992]], he contributed to Smith leading the league with 1,713 rushing yards and 18 rushing [[touchdown]]s. He missed the playoffs because of a right knee injury he suffered in the season finale against the [[Chicago Bears]] and was not a part of [[Super Bowl XXVII]]. He was replaced with [[Derek Tennell]].{{Cite web |title=Cowboys Sign Tennell |url=https://newsok.com/article/2416970/cowboys-sign-tennell? |access-date=February 5, 2018}} In [[1993 NFL season|1993]], he was placed on the [[injured reserve list]] after fracturing his foot during a training camp passing drill against the [[Los Angeles Raiders]].{{Cite web |title=Cowboys without Roberts |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1842&dat=19930727&id=PIEgAAAAIBAJ&sjid=ascEAAAAIBAJ&pg=1415,3885332&hl=en |access-date=February 5, 2018}} He was eventually replaced with [[Scott Galbraith]]. On March 31, [[1994 NFL season|1994]], he was released after not being able to recover from his previous foot injury.{{Cite web |title=Cowboys release Roberts |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=861&dat=19940401&id=OjhOAAAAIBAJ&sjid=E0sDAAAAIBAJ&pg=5762,85152&hl=en |access-date=February 5, 2018}} ==Coaching career== Roberts transitioned to coaching ahead of the 1999 NCAA season when he was hired by [[Florida Atlantic University]] to serve as their running backs coach. He then transitioned into the school's wide receivers coach for the 2001 and 2002 seasons.{{cite web | title=Florida Atlantic University Athletics | website=Florida Atlantic University Athletics | date=August 30, 2025 | url=https://fausports.com/sports/football/roster/coaches/alfredo-roberts/606 | access-date=September 24, 2025}} In 2003, he was hired by his first NFL team, becoming the tight ends coach for the [[Jacksonville Jaguars]] for four seasons. Between 2007 and 2015, he was a tight ends coach for three different teams ([[Cleveland Browns]], [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]], [[Indianapolis Colts]]). He continued to coach at [[Carmel High School (Indiana)|Carmel High School]] before returning to the NFL to coach with the [[Los Angeles Chargers]] from 2017 until 2020.{{cite web | title=Alfredo Roberts | website=Pro Football History.com | date=March 17, 1965 | url=https://pro-football-history.com/coach/802/alfredo-roberts-bio | access-date=September 24, 2025}} On January 25, 2021, Roberts was hired by the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]], where he continues to be the team's tight ends coach as of [[2025 Pittsburgh Steelers season|2025]].{{cite web | last=Varley | first=Teresa | title=Steelers hire Roberts to coach tight ends | website=Steelers.com | date=January 25, 2021 | url=https://www.steelers.com/news/steelers-hire-roberts-to-coach-tight-ends | access-date=September 24, 2025}} On February 10, 2026, the [[New York Jets]] hired Roberts as their tight ends coach under offensive coordinator [[Frank Reich]].{{cite web |title=Jets Finalize Offensive Coaching Staff with Six Additions '''Alfred Anthony Anderson''' (born August 4, 1961) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[running back]] for eight seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL).

Anderson was born and raised in [[Waco, Texas]] and played scholastically at [[Richfield High School (Waco)|Richfield High School]].<ref name="PFR1">{{cite web|title=Alfred Anderson|publisher=Pro Football Reference|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/A/AndeAl00.htm|access-date=2011-04-11}}</ref> He played [[college football]] for the [[Baylor Bears football|Baylor Bears]],<ref name="NFL">{{cite web| url=https://www.nfl.com/players/alfred-anderson/ |title=Alfred Anderson Stats |website=NFL.com |access-date=May 29, 2024}}</ref> where, as a senior, he was honored by ''[[The Football News|Football News]]'' as a second-team [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]].<ref name="FN 1983">{{cite news |title=All-America |date=November 30, 1983 |newspaper=The Sioux City Journal |page=C2 |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/72113120/ |access-date=February 26, 2021 |via=Newspapers.com}}</ref>

Anderson was selected in the third round of the [[1984 NFL draft]] by the [[Minnesota Vikings]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=1984 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1984/draft.htm |access-date=2023-10-10 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> and spent his entire career with them.<ref name="PFA">{{Cite web |url=https://www.profootballarchives.com/playera/ande01000.html |title=Alfred Anderson Stats |website=Pro Football Archives |access-date=May 29, 2024 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231207045854/https://www.profootballarchives.com/playera/ande01000.html |archive-date=December 7, 2023}}</ref>

'''Allan Delon Ellis''' (August 19, 1951 – September 18, 2013) was an American professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[cornerback]] for nine seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[UCLA Bruins football|UCLA Bruins]]. In 1977, Ellis was named to his lone [[Pro Bowl]], and is the first [[Chicago Bears]] cornerback to be named.<ref>{{cite web|last=Mayer|first=Larry|url=http://www.chicagobears.com/news/article-1/Five-Bears-players-voted-to-Pro-Bowl/247b6291-c79f-44aa-827d-eb92cc1d40fe|title=Five Bears players voted to Pro Bowl|publisher=[[Chicago Bears]]|date=December 26, 2012|accessdate=December 26, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121230220353/http://www.chicagobears.com/news/article-1/Five-Bears-players-voted-to-Pro-Bowl/247b6291-c79f-44aa-827d-eb92cc1d40fe|archive-date=December 30, 2012|url-status=dead}}</ref>

On September 18, 2013, Ellis died in Chicago.<ref>{{cite web|last=Mayer|first=Larry|url=http://www.chicagobears.com/news/article-1/Allan-Ellis-passes-away-at-age-62/0163587f-805a-46e7-8ab6-65d1b50db3a3|title=Allan Ellis passes away at age 62|publisher=[[Chicago Bears]]|date=September 20, 2013|accessdate=September 20, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130922083621/http://www.chicagobears.com/news/article-1/Allan-Ellis-passes-away-at-age-62/0163587f-805a-46e7-8ab6-65d1b50db3a3|archive-date=September 22, 2013|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Offensive passing game coordinator | highlights = * [[Melberger Award]] (2009) | statleague = NFL | statlabel1 = [[Completion (American football)|Pass completions]] | statvalue1 = 11 | statlabel2 = [[Attempt|Passing attempts]] | statvalue2 = 15 | statlabel3 = [[Percentage|Completion percentage]] | statvalue3 = 71.4 | statlabel4 = [[Touchdowns|TD]]–[[Interceptions|INT]] | statvalue4 = 1–0 | statlabel5 = [[Passing yards]] | statvalue5 = 100 | statlabel6 = [[Passer rating]] | statvalue6 = 113.2 | regular_record = | playoff_record = | overall_record = | pfr = TannAl00 | pfrcoach = }} '''Alex Tanney''' (born November 11, 1987) is an American [[American football|football]] coach and former [[quarterback]] who serves as the offensive passing game coordinator for the [[Indianapolis Colts]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Monmouth Fighting Scots football|Monmouth Fighting Scots]] and signed as an undrafted free agent with the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] in 2012. Tanney was also a member of the [[Dallas Cowboys]], [[Cleveland Browns]], [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]], [[Tennessee Titans]], [[Buffalo Bills]], Colts, and [[New York Giants]] before retiring in 2020. Tanney began his coaching in 2021 as an offensive quality control coach with the Eagles under head coach [[Nick Sirianni]]. ==Early life== Tanney was a three-sport high school standout athlete at [[Lexington High School (Illinois)|Lexington High School]] in [[Lexington, Illinois]], where he finished as the school's all-time leading point scorer.{{citation needed|date=February 2023}} He was a two-time first-team Illinois All-State quarterback and led his team to the IHSA state semi-finals his senior year. Tanney was also named an All-State basketball player. As a junior and senior, he placed at the IHSA State Track and Field Finals. == College career == Tanney broke nearly every school record during his time at [[Monmouth College]]. As a freshman in 2007, his career began when he threw for 2,678 yards and 24 touchdowns. As a sophomore in 2008, Tanney broke the school record of single-season touchdown passes with 50. As a junior in 2009, Tanney collected 3,856 passing yards, 44 passing touchdowns and a rushing score, which led him to be named the [[Melberger Award]] winner as [[NCAA]] [[NCAA Division III|D-III]]'s top player. Tanney was responsible for more than 24 points per game, while also averaging 350.55 passing yards and 348.73 total yards per contest. Tanney [[redshirt (college sports)|redshirted]] during the 2010 season, with a shoulder injury he suffered in the second game against [[Grinnell College]].{{cite web|last=Trueblood |first=Mike |url=https://www.galesburg.com/story/sports/college/2010/09/23/tanney-s-season-over-at/44973136007/ |title=Tanney's season over at Monmouth, Scots play Saturday |website=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=September 23, 2010 |access-date=September 1, 2014}} In February 2011, Tanney became famous after posting in [[YouTube]] a football trick-shot video that went viral.{{cite web|last=Farmer |first=Sam |url=https://www.latimes.com/sports/la-sp-cowboys-alex-tanney-20130814-story.html |title=Dallas quarterback Alex Tanney's trick-shot video that was no trick |website=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=August 13, 2013 |access-date=September 1, 2014}} In July, [[History (U.S. TV channel)|History Channel]]'s ''[[Stan Lee's Superhumans]]'' filmed an episode featuring him.{{cite web|last=Frey |first=Aaron |url= http://www.galesburg.com/editors_pick/x1797082895/Fighting-Scots-QB-Tanney-to-be-featured-on-History-Channel |title=Fighting Scots QB Tanney to be featured on History Channel |publisher= |website=Galesburg.com |date=July 23, 2011 |access-date=September 1, 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20120331232916/http://www.galesburg.com/editors_pick/x1797082895/Fighting-Scots-QB-Tanney-to-be-featured-on-History-Channel |archive-date=March 31, 2012 }} As a senior, Tanney came back and threw for a career-high 3,867 yards along with 38 touchdowns. On October 29, 2011, in a game against [[Carroll University]], he set the NCAA record for all-time all-division career touchdown passes with 150, surpassing [[Jimmy Terwilliger]]'s record of 148. Tanney finished his collegiate career with 157 touchdown passes and has the second most passing yards in NCAA D-III history with 14,249. He won three Midwest Conference Offensive Player of the Year Awards along with numerous All-American Awards. == Professional career == === Kansas City Chiefs === Tanney signed a contract with the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] as an undrafted [[free agent]] on June 5, 2012.{{Cite web |last=Scott |first=Brandon |date=2012-06-05 |title=NFL Free Agency 2012: Kansas City Chiefs Sign QB Alex Tanney |url=https://kansascity.sbnation.com/kansas-city-chiefs/2012/6/5/3065448/nfl-free-agency-2012-kansas-city-chiefs-sign-qb-alex-tanney |access-date=2025-06-03 |website=SB Nation Kansas City |language=en}} He was placed on injured reserve with a finger injury on September 1. === Dallas Cowboys === On July 21, 2013, the [[Dallas Cowboys]] signed Tanney to their roster.{{Cite web |title=Jay Ratliff on Cowboys' PUP list; Demetress Bell signs |url=https://www.nfl.com/news/jay-ratliff-on-cowboys-pup-list-demetress-bell-signs-0ap1000000219303 |access-date=2023-04-28 |website=NFL.com |language=en-US}} On August 4, he played the entire second half of the Hall of Fame Game in [[Canton, Ohio]]. On August 29, Tanney played all but one series in the 24–6 loss against the [[Houston Texans]], where he posted 17-of-31 completions for 177 yards and an interception while being sacked seven times.{{Cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/blog/dallas-cowboys/post/_/id/4713733/alex-tanney-takes-a-pounding|title = Cowboys' Tanney takes a pounding|date = August 30, 2013}} In five preseason games, Tanney completed 40-of-73 attempts for 423 yards, a touchdown, and two interceptions. He was released on August 30,{{Cite news| url= https://www.espn.com/blog/nflnation/post/_/id/82798/cowboys-to-waive-qb-alex-tanney|title=Cowboys to waive QB Alex Tanney|date=August 30, 2013}} but was '''Allen Ray Aldridge Jr.'''<ref>{{Cite web|url = http://www.nfl.com/players/allenaldridge/profile?id=ALD410038|title = Allen Aldridge Stats, News and Video - OLB|website = [[NFL.com]]|access-date = December 2, 2010|archive-date = April 11, 2010|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20100411074740/http://www.nfl.com/players/allenaldridge/profile?id=ALD410038|url-status = live}}</ref> (May 30, 1972 – September 8, 2024) was an American professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] and [[long snapper]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Houston Cougars football|Houston Cougars]]. He was selected by the [[Denver Broncos]] in the second round of the [[1994 NFL draft]] and later won [[Super Bowl XXXII]] with the team over the [[Green Bay Packers]].

Aldridge also played for the [[Detroit Lions]] and [[Houston Texans]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://old.houstontexans.com/news/Transactions2000_2002.asp |title=Texans Transactions - Houston Texans |access-date=2010-12-09 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110712223453/http://old.houstontexans.com/news/Transactions2000_2002.asp |archive-date=2011-07-12 }}</ref>

==Professional career==
===Denver Broncos===
Aldridge was drafted by the [[Denver Broncos]] in the second round of the [[1994 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1994 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1994/draft.htm |access-date=2023-03-31 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en |archive-date=November 4, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181104234555/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1994/draft.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> He started at middle linebacker in [[Super Bowl XXXII]] against the [[Green Bay Packers]]. He played for them from 1994 to 1997. During the four years he started 45 of 64 games, recording 227 [[Tackle (football move)|tackles]] and 1.5 [[Quarterback sack|sacks]].

===Detroit Lions===
Aldridge signed with the [[Detroit Lions]] before the 1998 season. He played for the team from 1998 to 2001. In the fours years he started 59 of 64 games, recording 237 tackles, nine sacks and an [[interception]]. He also served as the Lions' [[long snapper]] for punt coverage.<ref>[https://archive.today/20120708203026/http://findarticles.com/p/articles/mi_m1208/is_15_225/ai_74800708/pg_2/ Find articles] </ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Texans Sign Free-Agent LB Aldridge |url=http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1P1-52891717.html |work=AP Online |date=May 10, 2002 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121105052043/http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1P1-52891717.html |archive-date=November 5, 2012}}</ref>

'''Alfonso Smith''' (born January 23, 1987) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[running back]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Kentucky Wildcats football|Kentucky Wildcats]] and was signed by the [[Arizona Cardinals]] as an [[undrafted free agent]] in 2010. He was also a member of the [[San Francisco 49ers]].

==Early life==
Smith was born January 23, 1987 in [[San Bernardino, California]]. He attended [[Waggener High School]] in [[Louisville, Kentucky]].<ref name="PFR">{{cite web |title=Alfonso Smith Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/S/SmitAl22.htm |access-date=June 21, 2025}}</ref>

==College career==
Smith played [[college football]] for the [[Kentucky Wildcats football|Kentucky Wildcats]] from 2005 to 2009, [[Redshirt (college sports)|redshirting]] his freshman year.<ref>{{cite web |title=Alfonso Smith |website=University of Kentucky athletics |url=https://ukathletics.com/sports/football/roster/player/alfonso-smith/ |access-date=June 21, 2025}}</ref> He played in a reserve role from 2006 to 2008 until he earned a place in the [[starting lineup]] in his fifth-year senior season.<ref>{{cite web |last=Cosby |first=Chip |title=Alfonso Smith is UK's No. 1 back |website=[[Lexington Herald-Leader]] |url=https://www.kentucky.com/sports/college/kentucky-sports/uk-football/article44005311.html |date=August 8, 2009 |access-date=June 21, 2025}}</ref> His college career was marked by a series of minor but recurring injuries.<ref>{{cite web |last=Urban |first=Darren |title=Alfonso's Opportunity |website=azcardinals.com |url=https://www.azcardinals.com/news/alfonso-s-opportunity-5561621 |date=August 22, 2011 |access-date=June 21, 2025}}</ref> A thumb injury limited his play time during his senior season.<ref>{{cite web |last=Cosby |first=Chip |title=Alfonso Smith is looking for a thumbs-up review in second halfQ+A |website=[[Lexington Herald-Leader]] |url=https://www.kentucky.com/sports/college/kentucky-sports/uk-football/article44012106.html |date=October 24, 2009 |access-date=June 21, 2025}}</ref> Smith played in 49 games at Kentucky, rushing 215 times for 974 yards and eight [[touchdown]]s. He added 30 [[Reception (gridiron football)|receptions]] for 322 yards and two touchdowns, 15 [[kick return]]s for 155 yards, as well as 28 tackles, one forced [[fumble]], and one fumble recovery on [[special teams]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Arizona Cardinals: Alfonso Smith |website=azcardinals.com |url=http://www.azcardinals.com/team/roster/Alfonso-Smith/7695762a-361a-43b6-809d-5cac1a9d0d6f |access-date=June 21, 2025 |archive-date=July 28, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110728153028/http://www.azcardinals.com/team/roster/Alfonso-Smith/7695762a-361a-43b6-809d-5cac1a9d0d6f |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Professional career==

===Arizona Cardinals===
After going unselected in the [[2010 NFL draft]], Smith signed with the [[Arizona Cardinals]] as an undrafted free agent.<ref>{{cite web |title=Smith Bided His Time |website=azcardinals.com |url=https://www.azcardinals.com/news/smith-bided-his-time-5961942 |access-date=June 21, 2025}}</ref> Smith played in 43 games over four seasons with the Cardinals, rushing 48 times for 156 yards and two [[touchdown]]s.<ref name=NBC>{{cite web |last=Crabtree |first=Curtis |title=49ers agree to terms with Alfonso Smith |website=[[NBC Sports]] |url=https://www.nbcsports.com/nfl/profootballtalk/rumor-mill/news/49ers-agree-to-terms-with-alfonso-smith |date=July 28, 2014 |access-date=June 21, 2025}}</ref><ref name="SI">{{cite web |title=49ers sign Alfonso Smith for depth at running back following injuries |website=[[Sports Illustrated]] |url=https://www.si.com/nfl/2014/07/29/san-francisco-49ers-sign-alfonso-smith-running-back-injuries |date=July 29, 2014 |access-date=June 21, 2025}}</ref>

===San Francisco 49ers===
On July 28, 2014, the [[San Francisco 49ers]] agreed to terms with Smith.<ref name="NBC" /><ref name="SI" /> He rushed seven times for 19 yards in six games in his single season with the team.<ref name="PFR" />

==Coaching career==
On June 21, 2017, Smith joined the staff of the [[Michigan Wolverines football|Michigan Wolverines]] as an assistant running backs coach.<ref>{{cite web |last=Snyder |first=Mark |title=Michigan adds ex-NFL running back Alfonso Smith as assistant RB coach |website=[[Detroit Free Press]] |url=https://www.freep.com/story/sports/college/university-michigan/wolverines/2017/06/21/michigan-football-alfonso-smith/415230001/ |date=June 21, 2017 |access-date=June 21, 2025}}</ref>

In 2019, Smith returned to his alma mater, Waggener High School, as an assistant coach of the school's football team. He worked under head coach Tye Lawson, his former teammate at Kentucky.<ref>{{cite web |last=Chernoff |first=Andrew |title=Former NFL player returns 'home' to Waggener |website=[[WLKY]] |url=https://www.wlky.com/article/former-nfl-player-returns-home-to-waggener/28440657 |date=July 18, 2019 |access-date=June 21, 2025}}</ref>

'''Alfonzo Dennard''' (born September 9, 1989) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[cornerback]] for the [[New England Patriots]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Nebraska Cornhuskers football|Nebraska Cornhuskers]], and was selected by the [[New England Patriots]] in the [[2012 NFL draft]].

==Early life==
Dennard excelled on both sides of the ball at [[Wilcox County High School]], and was Nebraska's first scholarship player from [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]] since 2001. As a junior, Dennard caught 45 passes for 840 yards and 12 touchdowns, while rushing 24 times for 240 yards and six touchdowns. On defense, he made 60 tackles and had six interceptions. In his senior season, Dennard played a leading role in helping Wilcox County and Coach Mark Ledford to a 13–2 record and state runner-up finish in Class A. Dennard made 53 [[tackle (football move)|tackles]], while picking off five passes as a [[cornerback]]. Offensively, Dennard caught 39 passes for 780 yards and scored 14 [[touchdowns]]. He also used his speed to help on special teams, returning two kickoffs and one punt for touchdowns. Dennard received first-team Class A all-state honors from the Georgia Sportswriters Association. Dennard played in the GACA North-South All-Star game. Regarded as a three-star recruit by [[Rivals.com]], Dennard chose Nebraska over [[North Carolina Tar Heels football|North Carolina]] and [[Troy Trojans football|Troy]], among others.<ref>https://sports.yahoo.com/usf/football/recruiting/player-Alfonzo-Dennard-62973 {{Dead link|date=August 2022}}</ref>

Dennard was also a contributor in [[track and field|track]] and [[high school basketball|basketball]]. He played [[point guard]] in basketball and used his speed in [[sprint (running)|sprint]] events in track. In 2008, he placed second in the regional meet in the [[long jump]] after posting a personal-best leap of 6.68 meters (21 feet, 9 inches),<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://ga.milesplit.com/meets/36315/results/66465|title = Region 2A Boys Meet 2008 - Full Results (Raw)}}</ref> and finished sixth in the state with a leap of 6.50 meters (21 feet, 3 inches).<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://ga.milesplit.com/meets/30624/results/67568|title = Georgia Olympics 2008 - Official Day 1 Results-Converted (Raw)}}</ref>

==College career==
As a junior in 2010, Dennard started 13 of 14 games and had 31 tackles and four [[interceptions]]. He was a second-team all-[[Big 12 Conference]] selection.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.big12sports.com/ViewArticle.dbml?DB_OEM_ID=10410&ATCLID=205038561|title=All-Big 12 Football Awards Announced|access-date=December 2, 2011|date=November 30, 2010|publisher=Big12Spots.com}}</ref> In his senior year in 2011, Dennard was an all-Big Ten first-team selection and earned the Big Ten's [[Big Ten Conference football individual honors#Tatum–Woodson Defensive Back of the Year|Tatum-Woodson Defensive Back of the Year]] award.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.omaha.com/article/20111128/BIGRED/711289861|title=A Good First Impression|last=Kaipust|first=Rich|date=November 28, 2011|access-date=December 2, 2011|publisher=Omaha.com|archive-url=https://archive.today/20120905212602/http://www.omaha.com/article/20111128/BIGRED/711289861|archive-date=September 5, 2012|url-status=dead}}</ref>

In his final game as a Cornhusker during the Capital One Bowl game, Dennard was ejected at the end of the first half for fighting with South Carolina wide receiver [[Alshon Jeffery]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://profootballtalk.nbcsports.com/2012/01/02/likely-first-round-picks-jeffery-dennard-ejected-for-bowl-game-fight/|title=Likely first-round picks Jeffery, Dennard ejected for bowl game fight|date=January 2, 2012|last=Smith|first=Michael David|access-date=April 24, 2012|publisher=NBC Sports}}</ref>

===New England Patriots===
====2012====
The [[New England Patriots]] selected Dennard in the seventh round (224th overall) of the [[2012 NFL draft]]. He was the 29th cornerback selected in the 2012 NFL draft.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2012 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2012/draft.htm |access-date=May 14, 2023 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>
{{external media
| video1 = [http://www.nfl.com/videos/nfl-first-draft/09000d5d8283e662/First-Draft-Alfonzo-Dennard First Draft: Alfonzo Dennard]
}}

On May 17, 2012, the Patriots signed Dennard to a four-year, [[United States dollar|$]]2.15 million contract that includes a [[signing bonus]] of $14,462.<ref>{{cite web| title=Spotrac.com: Alfonzo Dennard contract| url=http://www.spotrac.com/nfl/arizona-cardinals/alfonzo-dennard-10045/| access-date=April 27, 2018| website=Spotrac.com}}</ref>

He competed with [[Devin McCourty]], [[Kyle Arrington]], [[Ras-I Dowling]], [[Will Allen (cornerback)|Will Allen]], and [[Sterling Moore]] throughout training camp for the job as the starting cornerback while [[Aqib Talib]] served his four-game suspension to begin the season. Dennard suffered a hamstring injury and missed a bulk of training camp, but returned for the last preseason game.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.musketfire.com/2012/09/09/alfonzo-dennard-and-nick-mcdonald-ruled-out/amp/| title=Alfonzo Dennard and Nick McDonald ruled out| access-date=November 10, 2017| website=musketfire.com| archive-date=November 11, 2017| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171111095012/https://musketfire.com/2012/09/09/alfonzo-dennard-and-nick-mcdonald-ruled-out/amp/| url-status=dead}}</ref> Head coach [[Bill Belichick]] named Dennard the fifth cornerback on the Patriots' depth chart to begin the {{NFL Year|2012}} season, behind McCourty, Arrington, Dowling, and Moore.<ref>{{cite web| title=Ourlads.com: New England Patriots' depth chart: 10/01/2012| url=http://www.ourlads.com/nfldepthcharts/archive/136/NE| access-date=November 10, 2017| website=Ourlads.com}}</ref>

On October 7, 2012, Dennard made his professional regular-season debut after missing the first four games with a hamstring injury. He made one tackle and deflected a pass as the Patriots defeated the [[2012 Denver Broncos season|Denver Broncos]], 31–21.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.nesn.com/2012/10/alfonzo-dennard-doesnt-allow-reception-in-strong-debut-rotating-with-sterling-moore-in-patriots-win-.html|title=Alfonzo Dennard Doesn't Allow Reception in Strong Debut Rotating With Sterling Moore in Patriots Win Over Broncos|last=Keyd|first=Doug|date=October 8, 2012|access-date=October 9, 2012|publisher=New England Sports Network}}</ref> On October 21, 2012, he earned his first career start and recorded two solo tackles, defended a pass, and made his first career interception on a pass attempt by [[Mark Sanchez]], as the Patriots won, 29–26.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.bostonherald.com/blogs/sports/blitz/index.php/2012/10/22/alfonzo-dennard-says-first-career-interception-felt-pretty-good/|title=Alfonzo Dennard says first career interception 'felt pretty good'|date=October 22, 2012|access-date=December 4, 2012|publisher=BostonHerald.com}}</ref> The following week, Dennard made five solo tackles, deflected a pass, and intercepted a pass attempt by [[2012 St. Louis Rams season|St. Louis Rams']] quarterback [[Sam Bradford]], as the Patriots routed them 45–7.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.nesn.com/2012/10/devin-mccourty-alfonzo-dennards-improvements-beginning-to-solve-problems-in-patriots-secondary.html|title=Devin McCourty, Alfonzo Dennard's Improvements Beginning to Solve Problems in Patriots' Secondary|access-date=December 4, 2012|date=October 30, 2012|publisher=NESN.com}}</ref>

On November 18, 2012, Dennard collected four solo tackles and two pass deflections, and intercepted a pass from [[Andrew Luck]] during a 59–24 victory over the [[2012 Indianapolis Colts season|Indianapolis Colts]]. He returned the interception for an 87-yard touchdown, marking the first and only one of his career. Dennard missed Weeks 16–17 with a hamstring injury after starting seven of the last eight games. He finished his rookie season with 35 combined tackles (34 solo), eight pass deflections, three interceptions, and a touchdown in ten games and seven starts.<ref name="stats">{{cite web| title=NFL Player stats: Alfonzo Dennard| url=http://www.nfl.com/player/alfonzodennard/2532832/gamelogs?season=2012| access-date=November 10, 2017| website=[[NFL.com]]}}</ref> The [[2012 New England Patriots season|New England Patriots]] finished first atop the [[AFC East]] with a 12–4 record and received a playoff berth.

On January 13, 2013, Dennard started his first career playoff game and recorded three combined tackles and a forced fumble during the 41–28 victory over the [[2012 Houston Texans season|Houston Texans]]. The following week, he started in the [[AFC Championship]] against the [[2012 Baltimore Ravens season|Baltimore Ravens]] and made two tackles in their 28-13 loss.<ref name="stats"/>

====2013====
Dennard returned to the New England Patriots' training camp and competed with Ras-I Dowling, Kyle Arrington, and [[Logan Ryan]] for the starting cornerback role. He was named the starting cornerback, opposite Aqib Talib, to begin the regular season.<ref>{{cite web| title=Ourlads.com: New England Patriots' depth chart: 10/01/2013| url=http://www.ourlads.com/nfldepthcharts/archive/148/NE| access-date=November 11, 2017| website=ourlads.com}}</ref>

He started the [[2013 New England Patriots season|New England Patriots']] season-opener against the [[2013 Buffalo Bills season|Buffalo Bills]] and collected three solo tackles and a pass deflection in their 23-21 victory. The next game, Dennard recorded a tackle, a pass deflection, and intercepted a pass attempt by [[Geno Smith]], as the Patriots defeated the [[2013 New York Jets season|New York Jets]] 13-10. On October 27, 2013, Dennard earned a season-high nine solo tackles during a 27-17 win against the [[2013 Miami Dolphins season|Miami Dolphins]]. He missed Week 11 with a knee injury and had [[Meniscus (anatomy)|meniscus]] [[arthroscopy]] a few days after.<ref>{{cite web| title=Alfonzo Dennard moving well at practice despite reportedly having knee surgery| url=https://nesn.com/2013/11/alfonzo-dennard-moving-well-at-practice-despite-reportedly-having-knee-surgery/| access-date=November 11, 2013| website=nesn.com| author=Doug Kyed| date=November 21, 2013}}</ref> Dennard recovered in time to play in their Week 12 victory over the [[2013 Denver Broncos season|Denver Broncos]]. He finished the 2013 season with a career-high 40 combined tackles (34 solo), eight pass deflections, and an interception. Dennard started nine games and was limited to 13 games after sustaining multiple injuries throughout the season.<ref name="stats"/>

The [[2013 New England Patriots season|New England Patriots]] finished first in the AFC East with a 12-4 record. On January 11, 2014, Dennard started in the Patriots' AFC divisional game and recorded two solo tackles, defended four pass, and had two key interceptions off of passes from [[2013 Indianapolis Colts season|Indianapolis Colts']] quarterback [[Andrew Luck]] during the Patriots' 43-22 victory. The following game, he collected three solo tackles as the Patriots' were eliminated from the playoffs after losing 26-16 to the [[2013 Denver Broncos season|Denver Broncos]] in the AFC Championship.

====2014====
He entered training camp in {{NFL Year|2014}} and faced stiff competition from [[Darrelle Revis]], Kyle Arrington, [[Brandon Browner]], and Logan Ryan for the vacant starting cornerback job left after the departure of [[Aqib Talib]]. Head coach [[Bill Belichick]] named him the starting cornerback, along with Darrelle Revis, to start the regular season.<ref>{{cite web| title=Ourlads.Com: New England Patriots' depth chart: 10/01/2014| url=http://www.ourlads.com/nfldepthcharts/archive/161/NE| access-date=November 11, 2017|  website=Ourlads.com}}</ref>

Dennard started the [[2014 New England Patriots season|New England Patriots']] season-opener at the [[2014 Miami Dolphins season|Miami Dolphins]] and recorded two solo tackles, deflected a pass, and intercepted a pass attempt by [[Ryan Tannehill]], as the Patriots lost 20-33. He went on to miss Weeks 2-4 after sustaining a shoulder injury.<ref>{{cite web| title=Rob Gronkowski, Alfonzo Dennard removed from injury report| url=https://www.bostonherald.com/sports/patriots_nfl/the_blitz/2014/10/rob_gronkowski_alfonzo_dennard_removed_from_injury_report| access-date=November 11, 2017| website=Bostonherald.com| author=Jeff Howe| date=October 8, 2014| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171112131800/http://www.bostonherald.com/sports/patriots_nfl/the_blitz/2014/10/rob_gronkowski_alfonzo_dennard_removed_from_injury_report| archive-date=November 12, 2017| url-status=dead}}</ref> On October 12, 2014, he recorded a season-high five solo tackles during the Patriots' 37-22 victory over the [[2014 Buffalo Bills season|Buffalo Bills]]. The following week, Dennard collected five combined tackles in a 27-25 victory against the [[2014 New York Jets season|New York Jets]]. A knee injury kept Dennard from playing in Week 8-9 and 11. After having minimal playing time is Weeks 12-13, Dennard missed the remainder of the season with a hamstring injury, including the playoffs and [[Super Bowl XLIX]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.scores.espn.go.com/nfl/boxscore?gameId=340111017|title=Scores for January 11th, 2014|date=January 12, 2014|access-date=January 12, 2014|work=ESPN.com|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140112084215/http://scores.espn.go.com/nfl/boxscore?gameId=340111017|archive-date=January 12, 2014|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web| title= Patriots List 18 Players On Injury Report|url=http://929theticket.com/patriots-list-18-players-on-injury-report/| access-date=November 12, 2017| website=929theticket.com| author=Clem LeBree| date=December 27, 2014}}</ref> He finished the season with 15 combined tackles (13 solo), one pass deflection, and an interception in six games and four starts.<ref name="stats"/>

The [[2014 New England Patriots season|New England Patriots]] finished the 2014 season atop the AFC East with a 12–4 record and went on to defeat the [[2014 Indianapolis Colts season|Indianapolis Colts]] 45–7 and then had a 28–24 win over the defending [[Super Bowl XLVIII|Super Bowl]] champion [[2014 Seattle Seahawks season|Seattle Seahawks]].

On May 5, 2015, Dennard was waived by the Patriots. They opted to waive Dennard even though they lost Darrelle Revis, Brandon Browner, and Kyle Arrington in free agency.
Multiple off-the-field incidents and injuries during his time with the Patriots were the main factors of his release.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bostonherald.com/sports/patriots_nfl/the_blitz/2015/05/alfonzo_dennard_released_by_patriots |title=Alfonzo Dennard released by Patriots| first=Jeff|last=Howe|newspaper=The Boston Globe|date=May 5, 2015|access-date=May 5, 2015}}</ref>

===Arizona Cardinals===
On May 6, 2015, Dennard was claimed off waivers by the [[Arizona Cardinals]].<ref>{{cite web|last1=Wesseling|first1=Chris|title=Alfonzo Dennard claimed by Arizona Cardinals|url=https://www.nfl.com/news/alfonzo-dennard-claimed-by-arizona-cardinals-0ap3000000491479|work=NFL.com|access-date=May 6, 2015}}</ref> The Cardinals released him on July 29, 2015.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/blog/arizona-cardinals/post/_/id/15016/cardinals-place-jermaine-gresham-on-pup-cut-alfonzo-dennard|title=Cardinals place Jermaine Gresham on PUP, cut Alfonzo Dennard|date=July 29, 2015|last=Weinfuss|first=Josh|access-date=July 29, 2015|work=ESPN.com}}</ref>

===Baltimore Brigade===
On January 16, 2017, it was announced that Dennard was among the first five players signed to the [[Baltimore Brigade]] of the [[Arena Football League]].<ref name="baltimoreafl">{{Cite web |url=http://www.baltimoreafl.com/articles/baltimore-arena-football-team-announces-first-signings |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170118032228/http://www.baltimoreafl.com/articles/baltimore-arena-football-team-announces-first-signings |url-status=dead |archive-date=January 18, 2017 |title=Baltimore Arena Football Team Announces First Signings |date=January 16, 2017 |publisher=[[Baltimore Brigade]] }}</ref>

===Saskatchewan Roughriders===
Dennard signed with the [[Saskatchewan Roughriders]] on April 25, 2017.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.riderville.com/2017/04/25/rider-transactions-april-25th/ | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170805020612/https://www.riderville.com/2017/04/25/rider-transactions-april-25th/ | url-status=dead | archive-date=August 5, 2017 | title=RIDER TRANSACTIONS- APRIL 25TH | publisher=riderville.com | date=April 25, 2017 | access-date=August 4, 2017}}</ref> He was released by the Roughriders on June 12, 2017.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.cfl.ca/transactions/ | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170804202744/https://www.cfl.ca/transactions/ | url-status=dead | archive-date=August 4, 2017 | title=CFL TRANSACTIONS | publisher=cfl.ca | access-date=August 4, 2017}}</ref>
